name: Tremella mushroom

lead: Tremella, or snow fungus, is an edible gelatinous fungus whose polysaccharide extracts are used in Asian skincare as a plant alternative to hyaluronic acid. People use it for skin that stays hydrated, looks plumper and shows softer fine lines.

The chain is water-holding: its polysaccharides are described as absorbing and holding water at the skin surface, so skin feels and looks more hydrated. A patent also reports inhibition of melanin formation, which is why some products pitch it for brightening. The sources found are encyclopedic descriptions and patents; clinical trials were not found.

paras: Used in essences, serums, creams and masks, applied to clean skin as a hydrating step under moisturiser. It is often combined with other humectants such as hyaluronic acid or glycerin. Users commonly report skin feeling more hydrated right after application, with a more lasting effect from consistent daily use.
No skincare safety data were found. The fungus itself is a long-established food in Chinese cuisine, and topical products carry standard irritation precautions.

angle.text: Tremella polysaccharides are used in Asian skincare as a plant-based alternative to hyaluronic acid, holding water at the skin surface so skin looks plumper and fine lines look softer. A patent also describes it reducing melanin formation for a brighter tone.

lead: Tremella fuciformis, known as snow fungus or silver ear, is an edible white gelatinous fungus cultivated commercially in China and used in Chinese cuisine and traditional medicine.[1] Extracts, especially polysaccharides, appear in skincare products from China, Korea and Japan, where they are marketed as moisture-retaining and anti-wrinkle.[1]
Patent literature describes a hot-water-extracted Tremella polysaccharide with water-holding capacity and melanin-inhibiting effects.[2] No published clinical trials of topical Tremella were found.

paras: The fungus forms white, frond-like fruit bodies up to about 7 cm across and grows as a parasitic yeast on other fungi on dead broadleaf wood. Berkeley described it in 1856 from Brazilian collections.[1] It has been cultivated in China since at least the 19th century, and a modern dual-culture method with its host fungus is now used; estimated Chinese output in 1997 was 130,000 tonnes.[1]

Traditionally it is used in sweet soups and desserts and, in traditional Chinese medicine, is valued for nourishing the lungs and increasing yin.[1] In cosmetics, extracts are reported to retain moisture, raise superoxide dismutase levels and have anti-inflammatory effects; Wikipedia presents these as reported claims rather than established results.[1]

A 2006 US patent describes a Tremella polysaccharide for skin care with moisturizing and melanin-formation-inhibiting effects, and a 2008 patent describes use for constipation.[2][3] Patents are descriptions of claimed inventions, not clinical evidence.
No studies found on topical Tremella in humans. Related material is limited to patent descriptions and a 2021 review of Tremella polysaccharides cited by Wikipedia.[1][2]
